query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Modifying the integrity of the native oxide film on pristine Q235 steel determines its susceptibility to corrosion: deliberately removing or compromising the oxide film will accelerate corrosion initiation and propagation in harsh, chloride-rich environments—especially at elevated temperatures—while enhancing the oxide film via passivation will delay these processes.
generation.material_initial_state: Pristine Q235 steel with its naturally formed, indigenous oxide film.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled pre-treatments to alter the oxide film: one set undergoes mild chemical etching to remove or thin the native oxide, and another set receives a passivation treatment aimed at forming a denser, more protective oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a harsh environment replicating a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution with controlled humidity at two temperature regimes: room temperature (~25°C) and elevated temperature (~75°C).
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and chemical composition of the surface oxide film mediate the diffusion of aggressive ions and govern the electrochemical reactions at the metal/oxide interface.
generation.mechanism: A continuous, robust native oxide film acts as a barrier to electron and ion transfer, inhibiting local anodic dissolution. When this film is compromised (e.g., via etching), the underlying metal becomes exposed, enabling localized corrosion (pitting) and overall degradation, an effect that is amplified by higher temperatures accelerating film breakdown and reaction kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, the etched specimens will exhibit higher corrosion current densities, greater weight loss, and more pronounced pitting—especially at 75°C. In contrast, specimens receiving the passivation treatment will show lower corrosion rates and improved surface integrity relative to the untreated reference.
generation.baseline: Untreated pristine Q235 steel with its native oxide film exposed to the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under laboratory-controlled conditions with fixed chloride concentration, humidity, and temperature ranges; effects in more variable or real-world conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in corrosion rates between treatments are not predetermined and may be influenced by additional microstructural factors beyond the oxide film. The interplay between oxide film modifications and inherent steel heterogeneities also remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples: (1) untreated (with native oxide intact), (2) oxide-removed via mild chemical etching, and (3) passivated to enhance the oxide film. Subject all sets to identical exposure in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under controlled high-humidity conditions at both room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (~75°C). Monitor corrosion using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), Tafel polarization measurements, weight loss analysis over fixed intervals, and microscopic surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to assess oxide film integrity and corrosion morphology.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion current densities (from Tafel curves)
Surface morphology and chemical composition (via SEM and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant differences in corrosion rate (current densities, impedance values), weight loss, or surface pitting/morphology are observed among the etched, passivated, and untreated samples under both temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that the native oxide film’s integrity governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in Q235 steel is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nevertheless, although the passivation film can improve the corrosion resistance, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating will inevitably be subjected to some local corrosion as with other corrosion-resistant alloys. Owing to the more negative the potential of the metal standard electrode, the easier it is to lose electrons and dissolve. Moreover, for the alloy of this paper, the standard potential of Nb (−1.1 V) and Cr (−0.74 V) is significantly lower than that of Fe (−0.44 V), Ni (−0.25 V) and Co (−0.28 V) [,]. Therefore, during the electrochemical experiment, once the local passivation film is destroyed, the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr is preferentially corroded as an anode, and the dendritic phase rich in Co, Ni, and Fe is protected as a cathode, which results in selective corrosion on the surface of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating. Furthermore, as the pitting behavior continues, the adjacent interdendritic regions are completely corroded, causing catastrophic corrosion (Figure 7b). Similarly, this phenomenon of selective corrosion was observed in CrMnFeCoNi HEA [] and AlCoCrFeNi [].

For the Mo-HEA coating on the 235JR and 316L substrates, no corrosion damage was observed after the exposure in the aerated testing. It was, however, observed that the Mo-HEA coating had formed a partial, Cr-O rich, passive layer on the surface as seen in Figure 9. The oxide passive film resulted from the exposure to the oxygen in the aerated fluid, but to some surprise, the Cr-O film was always discontinuous on the surface and did not cover the whole surface of the Mo-HEA coating. The reason for the discontinuous oxide layer on the surface is not fully understood, but one explanation is that Cr concentration gradients that are present in the bulk coating near the surface and sluggish diffusion rate of Cr from the high entropy material to the surface could result in slow oxide layer formation in some locations. Hence, a propagating growth of the oxide film to become more continuous on the surface could be attained by longer exposure periods in the aerated fluid, but this should be verified with longer exposure periods. decision.trend: Over the past few years, researchers working on high-performance alloys have progressively moved from macroscopic descriptions of corrosion rates to mechanistic studies that isolate the effects of elemental dissolution and surface film stability. Early work identified broad correlations between environmental parameters and overall degradation, while later studies—such as PMC6908586—focused on how the selective loss of elements (e.g., Mn) and the concurrent retention or formation of protective surface oxides influence corrosion behavior under controlled high‐temperature environments. Although these studies have been conducted primarily on high‐entropy and related complex alloys, the method of isolating a single cause (e.g., passivation failure vs. selective dissolution) remains a valuable paradigm.
decision.unsolved: For conventional materials like Q235 steel in its pristine, pre-exposure state, the mechanistic trigger that leads to either the onset or suppression of corrosion under harsh conditions remains unresolved. In particular, the roles of the native oxide film integrity, underlying microstructural features, and their interplay with variables such as aggressive chloride ions and temperature gradients have not been isolated and definitively tested with decisive falsification criteria.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the integrity of the native oxide layer via controlled pre-treatment (e.g., mild chemical etching versus passivation protocols) while independently modulating environmental aggressiveness (chloride concentration and humidity) and temperature (room vs. elevated conditions)
decision.why: This step directly isolates the effect of the pre-existing oxide film on corrosion initiation in Q235 steel relative to an untreated reference. Drawing on trends from studies like PMC6908586 that pinpoint specific elemental and surface film effects, the proposed experiment offers a clear testable mechanistic hypothesis: if the native oxide film governs corrosion onset, then its deliberate removal or modification will lead to a statistically predictable acceleration (or suppression if a more protective film is formed) of corrosion under controlled conditions, with a decisive falsification achieved if no differential response is observed.

families.principle: Isolate and quantify the influence of specific environmental and material variables on corrosion kinetics and film formation in a macroscopic, well-controlled setting.

cues_against: does not directly capture atomic‐scale transient phenomena
families.best_lever: Systematically vary the oxide film’s thickness or composition and modulate environmental aggressiveness (e.g., Cl- concentration, humidity, temperature) to observe deviations in corrosion onset relative to the untreated sample.

families.principle: Integrate controlled experiments with complementary simulations to bridge macroscopic observations and microscale mechanisms, thereby enabling hypothesis testing with both empirical data and mechanistic models.
cues_against: increased complexity and resource demands might be a drawback if a simpler experiment already sufficiently isolates the mechanism
families.best_lever: Design an experiment that controls key environmental variables while simultaneously conducting simulations to model oxide film dynamics; use the simulation to identify parameter sensitivities that can then be directly tested experimentally against the untreated reference.

families.principle: Employ real-time, high-resolution imaging or spectroscopic techniques to directly observe the evolving corrosion process and associated transient changes in the oxide or microstructure under controlled conditions.
cues_for: harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures require dynamic measurement
cues_against: if the mechanism is predominantly macroscopic or readily isolable by controlled experiments, the complexity of in situ methods might be unnecessary
families.best_lever: Utilize in situ environmental TEM or electrochemical AFM to capture real-time changes at the steel surface during exposure, isolating the formation or suppression of corrosive features compared to the reference.

families.principle: Model the corrosion process from atomic or microstructural scales to predict how variations in initial oxide chemistry or microstructure influence corrosion kinetics, providing insights inaccessible to direct measurements.
cues_for: potential insights into the underlying pathways at a scale hard to measure directly

simulations may not fully capture macroscale boundary conditions
families.best_lever: Implement phase-field or molecular dynamics simulations focusing on the evolution of surface oxide defects and microstructural heterogeneity to predict conditions under which corrosion initiation is either promoted or suppressed.
